points_json.example: Billions of neurons in your brain are firing right now to let you read this sentence.
points_json.point: A neuron is a nerve cell — the basic communication unit of the nervous system. The human brain has about 86 billion neurons, each connecting to thousands of others, forming trillions of connections.

points_json.example: Like a tree's branches catching sunlight, dendrites catch incoming messages from other neurons.
points_json.point: A neuron has three main parts. Dendrites receive signals from other neurons. The cell body (soma) processes these signals. The axon carries the outgoing message away toward other neurons.

points_json.example: Multiple sclerosis damages myelin, which is why patients feel weakness and numbness — signals travel too slowly.
points_json.point: Many axons are wrapped in a myelin sheath, a fatty layer made by glial cells. Myelin insulates the axon and speeds up signal travel, like insulation on an electric wire.

points_json.example: Astrocytes clean up extra chemicals around neurons, keeping the brain's environment safe and balanced.
points_json.point: Glial cells support neurons — they feed them, clean waste, form myelin, and fight infections. Glia actually outnumber neurons in the brain, about 10 to 1 by some counts.

points_json.example: Touching a hot stove sends a signal through sensory neurons to your spinal cord, and motor neurons pull your hand back.
points_json.point: There are three neuron types. Sensory (afferent) neurons carry information from senses to the brain and spinal cord. Motor (efferent) neurons carry commands to muscles. Interneurons connect neurons to each other inside the brain and spinal cord.

points_json.example: After a spinal cord injury, damaged axons in the central nervous system regrow very poorly, which is why recovery is so hard.
points_json.point: Unlike skin cells, most neurons do not divide and replace themselves. However, new neurons can grow in some areas like the hippocampus — this is called neurogenesis.

points_json.example: A motor neuron controlling your leg muscle can be over a meter long, while a brain interneuron may be tiny.
points_json.point: Neurons vary greatly in size and shape. Some axons are extremely long, while interneurons in the brain are very short. Shape matches function.

points_json.example: The tiny gaps between the axon terminal of one neuron and the dendrite of the next are where communication happens.
points_json.point: Axon terminals (terminal buttons) sit at the end of the axon. When a signal arrives, they release chemicals called neurotransmitters into the synapse to pass the message to the next neuron.

summary: The brain's building block explained simply — parts of a neuron, glial cells, neuron types, and how they connect.
title: The Neuron in Depth

points_json.example: Before a signal fires, the neuron sits quietly at -70 mV, like a sprinter waiting in the starting blocks.
points_json.point: At rest, a neuron has a resting potential of about -70 millivolts — the inside is negative compared to the outside. Sodium ions crowd outside, potassium ions sit inside, maintained by the sodium-potassium pump.

points_json.example: A light tap on your arm may not fire pain neurons, but a hard pinch crosses the threshold and you feel pain.
points_json.point: A stimulus must push the neuron past the threshold (about -55 mV) to fire. Weak stimuli that don't reach threshold cause nothing — this is why small touches feel different from painful ones.

points_json.example: Like a row of dominoes, sodium channels open one after another down the axon, each triggering the next.
points_json.point: Once threshold is crossed, sodium channels fly open and positive sodium rushes in — this is depolarization, spiking the charge up to about +40 mV. This wave travels down the axon.

points_json.example: After the peak, potassium rushes out and the neuron briefly dips below its resting level before recovering.
points_json.point: Then potassium channels open, potassium flows out, and the neuron repolarizes back toward rest. It briefly overshoots below -70 mV — this is hyperpolarization — before the pump restores balance.

points_json.example: Right after firing, a neuron cannot fire again for a split second, which stops signals from bouncing backward.
points_json.point: The refractory period is a brief recovery time after firing when the neuron cannot fire again (absolute) or needs a stronger push (relative). This keeps the signal moving in one direction.

points_json.example: A gun either fires or it doesn't — there is no half-shot. Neurons work the same way.
points_json.point: The all-or-none law: a neuron fires at full strength or not at all. A stronger stimulus doesn't make a bigger signal — it makes the neuron fire more frequently.

points_json.example: Myelinated axons can carry signals at 120 meters per second — fast enough to pull your hand from fire before you consciously feel pain.
points_json.point: Myelin speeds transmission hugely. The signal jumps between gaps in the myelin (nodes of Ranvier) in saltatory conduction, instead of crawling along the whole axon.

points_json.example: Local anesthetics like lidocaine block sodium channels, so pain signals never start — the area goes numb.
points_json.point: Many drugs work by targeting the action potential. Local anesthetics block sodium channels. Some toxins, like pufferfish poison, do the same thing — which is why they are deadly.

summary: How neurons fire — resting potential, threshold, depolarization, and the all-or-none law, step by step.
title: Action Potential Explained

points_json.example: Two neurons never actually touch — they whisper across a tiny gap called the synaptic cleft.
points_json.point: A synapse is the junction where one neuron passes its message to the next. It has three parts: the presynaptic terminal, the tiny synaptic cleft (gap), and the postsynaptic membrane of the receiving neuron.

points_json.example: Like popping bubble wrap, calcium entering the terminal makes vesicles burst and spill their chemicals into the gap.
points_json.point: When an action potential reaches the terminal, calcium channels open. Calcium rushes in and tells synaptic vesicles (tiny sacs) to release neurotransmitter molecules into the cleft.

points_json.example: A key fits only its own lock — serotonin cannot activate a dopamine receptor.
points_json.point: Neurotransmitters cross the gap and bind to receptor sites on the next neuron, like a key fitting a lock. Each receptor accepts only specific neurotransmitters.

points_json.example: Excitatory signals push the neuron toward firing; inhibitory signals hold it back — the neuron listens to both sides before deciding.
points_json.point: Some synapses are excitatory (EPSPs push toward firing) and some are inhibitory (IPSPs push away from firing). The receiving neuron sums up all inputs — if excitation wins, it fires.

points_json.example: Prozac blocks serotonin reuptake, leaving more serotonin in the gap for longer — which lifts mood in many patients.
points_json.point: After signaling, the neurotransmitter must be cleared: sucked back into the sender (reuptake), broken down by enzymes, or simply drifting away. Many antidepressants work by blocking reuptake.

points_json.example: Botox blocks acetylcholine release in facial muscles, which is why treated areas cannot wrinkle — the muscle never gets the signal.
points_json.point: Drugs and toxins hijack synapses. Botox blocks neurotransmitter release. Curare blocks receptors, causing paralysis. Understanding synapses explains how most brain drugs work.

points_json.example: A single neuron can receive thousands of synaptic inputs at once, weighing them all in milliseconds.
points_json.point: One neuron may have thousands of synapses on its dendrites and cell body. Integration of all these excitatory and inhibitory messages decides whether it fires.

points_json.example: In reflexes, electrical synapses let neurons share charge instantly through gap junctions — faster than chemical ones.
points_json.point: Most synapses are chemical, but some are electrical — direct channels (gap junctions) between neurons. These are super fast and found in reflex pathways and the heart.

summary: How neurons talk across the gap — vesicles, receptors, reuptake, and how drugs hijack the process.
title: Synapses and Neurotransmission

points_json.example: Turkey contains tryptophan, the building block of serotonin — though the 'sleepy after turkey' effect is mostly myth.
points_json.point: Serotonin is a neurotransmitter made from the amino acid tryptophan. It is produced mainly in the raphe nuclei of the brainstem and sent widely across the brain.

points_json.example: When serotonin signaling drops, people often feel flat, worried, and unable to enjoy things they once loved.
points_json.point: Serotonin helps regulate mood, sleep, appetite, aggression, and pain perception. Low serotonin activity is linked to depression, anxiety, OCD, and impulsive behavior — though the link is more complex than 'low serotonin equals depression.'

points_json.example: Prozac (fluoxetine) was the first famous SSRI — it made depression treatment much safer than older drugs.
points_json.point: SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) block the reuptake of serotonin, leaving more of it active in synapses. They are first-line treatments for depression, anxiety, OCD, and PTSD.

points_json.example: About 90 percent of the body's serotonin is in the gut, controlling digestion — the 'second brain' in your belly.
points_json.point: Most serotonin is actually outside the brain, mainly in the intestines where it controls gut movement. This gut-brain connection is why stomach problems and mood often go together.

points_json.example: Ecstasy (MDMA) floods the brain with serotonin, causing intense warmth and bonding — followed by a harsh crash as supplies run dry.
points_json.point: Drugs like LSD and ecstasy act on serotonin receptors. LSD mimics serotonin at certain receptors, causing hallucinations. MDMA forces massive serotonin release.

points_json.example: People in dark northern winters often feel low as sunlight drops — light therapy helps by boosting serotonin activity.
points_json.point: Sunlight exposure increases serotonin production. This partly explains seasonal affective disorder (winter depression) and why bright light therapy helps.

points_json.example: Taking too many serotonergic drugs together can cause serotonin syndrome — confusion, fever, tremors — a medical emergency.
points_json.point: Too much serotonin is dangerous. Serotonin syndrome happens when drugs combine to overload the system, causing agitation, high fever, and muscle rigidity. It needs urgent treatment.

points_json.example: SSRIs usually take 2 to 6 weeks to work — the delay involves slow receptor changes, not just more serotonin.
points_json.point: Antidepressants don't work instantly because the brain needs time to adapt — receptors adjust and new neurons may grow in the hippocampus. Patience matters in treatment.

summary: The mood chemical in depth — what serotonin does, how SSRIs work, and the gut-brain surprise.
title: Serotonin: Mood and More

points_json.example: The first bite of chocolate cake after a long diet feels amazing — that's dopamine marking it as worth seeking again.
points_json.point: Dopamine is the brain's reward and motivation chemical. The mesolimbic pathway (from the VTA to the nucleus accumbens) fires when we get rewards — food, praise, or an unexpected win.

points_json.example: Slot machines pay out unpredictably, which spikes dopamine harder than steady rewards — that's why gambling is so addictive.
points_json.point: Dopamine responds most to unexpected rewards and cues predicting them. This 'prediction error' signal is why surprises thrill us and why gambling and social media notifications hook us.

points_json.example: Research shows dopamine drives 'wanting' (craving, seeking) more than 'liking' (pleasure) — addicts crave drugs they no longer enjoy.
points_json.point: Scientist Kent Berridge showed dopamine fuels wanting rather than liking. This explains addiction: intense craving even when the drug brings little pleasure anymore.

points_json.example: Parkinson's patients lose dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra, causing tremors and stiffness — L-DOPA replaces the missing dopamine.
points_json.point: Dopamine also controls movement. In Parkinson's disease, dopamine-producing neurons die, causing shaking, rigidity, and slow movement. L-DOPA treatment restores dopamine.

points_json.example: Antipsychotic drugs block dopamine receptors, calming hallucinations — but can cause Parkinson-like stiffness as a side effect.
points_json.point: Schizophrenia is linked to excess dopamine activity in some brain pathways. Drugs that block dopamine D2 receptors reduce hallucinations and delusions.

points_json.example: Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake, flooding synapses — the intense high is followed by a crash as the system depletes.
points_json.point: Addictive drugs hijack dopamine: cocaine and amphetamines flood synapses with it, while opioids and alcohol trigger its release indirectly. The brain then needs the drug to feel normal.

points_json.example: A child with ADHD given a stimulant can suddenly sit still and focus — the drug boosts the dopamine their brain lacks.
points_json.point: ADHD involves dopamine dysregulation in attention circuits. Stimulant medicines (like methylphenidate) increase dopamine availability, which paradoxically calms hyperactivity and sharpens focus.

summary: The motivation molecule — reward pathways, addiction, Parkinson's, schizophrenia, and ADHD.
title: Dopamine: Reward and Motivation

points_json.example: Hearing a strange noise at night, your heart pounds and every sense sharpens — norepinephrine is on duty.
points_json.point: Norepinephrine (noradrenaline) is the alertness chemical, released mainly by the locus coeruleus in the brainstem. It wakes the brain up and focuses attention.

points_json.example: In danger, norepinephrine and adrenaline prepare the body: heart races, breathing quickens, pupils widen — the fight-or-flight response.
points_json.point: During stress, norepinephrine drives the sympathetic nervous system's fight-or-flight response. Blood flows to muscles, digestion pauses, and the mind locks onto the threat.

points_json.example: A student slightly nervous before an exam performs better than one totally calm or one panicking.
points_json.point: The Yerkes-Dodson law: moderate arousal gives the best performance. Too little norepinephrine means drowsiness; too much means panicked, scattered thinking.

points_json.example: Musicians with stage fright take beta-blockers to stop shaking hands and racing hearts before performances.
points_json.point: Beta-blockers block norepinephrine's effects on the body, calming physical anxiety symptoms like trembling and fast heartbeat. They don't sedate the mind — just the body.

points_json.example: Effexor (venlafaxine), an SNRI, boosts both serotonin and norepinephrine and helps depression with low energy and poor focus.
points_json.point: Low norepinephrine is linked to depression, especially with fatigue and concentration problems. SNRIs raise both serotonin and norepinephrine levels.

points_json.example: Norepinephrine follows a daily rhythm — lowest during sleep, rising before you wake to pull you into alertness.
points_json.point: This chemical helps run the sleep-wake cycle. It drops during sleep (especially REM) and surges in the morning. Disrupted rhythms affect mood and attention.

points_json.example: Veterans with PTSD given prazosin (which blocks norepinephrine) often report fewer trauma nightmares.
points_json.point: PTSD involves an overactive norepinephrine system — constant hyperarousal and startle. Drugs dampening this system can reduce nightmares and flashbacks.

summary: The alertness chemical — fight-or-flight, attention, the Yerkes-Dodson law, and its role in depression and PTSD.
title: Norepinephrine and Stress

points_json.example: GABA is the brain's brake pedal — without it, neural activity would spin out of control into seizures.
points_json.point: GABA is the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter. It calms neural activity by making neurons less likely to fire, preventing overstimulation.

points_json.example: People with low GABA activity often feel tense, restless, and unable to switch off worry.
points_json.point: Low GABA function is linked to anxiety disorders, insomnia, and epilepsy. Boosting GABA calms the mind — which is why so many anti-anxiety drugs target it.

points_json.example: A glass of wine relaxes you because alcohol enhances GABA — but heavy drinking disrupts the balance badly.
points_json.point: Alcohol and benzodiazepines (like Valium) enhance GABA's calming effect. That's why they reduce anxiety and cause drowsiness — and why mixing them can dangerously suppress breathing.

points_json.example: Glutamate strengthens the connections you use — every time you practice piano, glutamate helps wire the skill in.
points_json.point: Glutamate is the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter and is essential for learning and memory. Long-term potentiation (LTP), the basis of memory, depends on glutamate receptors.

points_json.example: During a stroke, dying neurons dump glutamate, overexciting neighbors to death — this 'excitotoxicity' spreads the damage.
points_json.point: Too much glutamate is toxic. In stroke and brain injury, excess glutamate overstimulates neurons until they die. This excitotoxicity is a major treatment target.

points_json.example: Ketamine blocks NMDA glutamate receptors and can lift severe depression within hours — a breakthrough finding.
points_json.point: Glutamate acts heavily through NMDA receptors. Ketamine, an NMDA blocker, produces rapid antidepressant effects, opening a whole new direction in depression research.

points_json.example: Epilepsy often reflects a broken GABA-glutamate balance — too much excitation, too little inhibition.
points_json.point: Seizures happen when excitation overwhelms inhibition. Many anti-epileptic drugs either boost GABA or dampen glutamate to restore the balance.

summary: The brain's brake and accelerator — how GABA calms, glutamate excites, and their balance shapes anxiety, memory, and seizures.
title: GABA and Glutamate

points_json.example: After a long run, many people feel a calm, happy glow — the famous 'runner's high' comes from endorphins.
points_json.point: Endorphins are the body's natural painkillers — 'endogenous morphine.' The brain releases them during exercise, stress, pain, and laughter to reduce suffering and lift mood.

points_json.example: Morphine and heroin hijack the same opioid receptors that endorphins use — but far more powerfully, causing addiction.
points_json.point: Endorphins bind to opioid receptors, the same ones targeted by morphine, heroin, and codeine. Natural endorphins are gentler and non-addictive; drugs overwhelm the system.

points_json.example: In studies, the placebo effect's pain relief disappears when patients get naloxone, an opioid blocker — proving endorphins were doing the work.
points_json.point: Believing a sugar pill is medicine can trigger real endorphin release and real pain relief. Blocking opioid receptors with naloxone wipes out the placebo effect.

points_json.example: Soldiers badly wounded in battle sometimes feel no pain until they reach safety — stress-triggered endorphins mask it.
points_json.point: Extreme stress triggers massive endorphin release, suppressing pain during emergencies. This survival mechanism lets injured people keep moving when it matters most.

points_json.example: Eating very spicy food hurts, then feels oddly good — the pain triggers endorphins, creating pleasure from the burn.
points_json.point: Spicy food activates pain receptors, and the brain answers with endorphins. That's why chili lovers describe a pleasurable rush after the burn.

points_json.example: Laughing hard with friends and gentle touch both release endorphins, strengthening social bonds.
points_json.point: Social behaviors release endorphins too — laughter, grooming in primates, and warm touch. This may be why friendship literally feels good and eases pain.

points_json.example: Acupuncture's pain relief may work partly because needle stimulation triggers endorphin release.
points_json.point: Research suggests acupuncture prompts the nervous system to release endorphins and other natural opioids, which may explain its pain-relieving effects.

points_json.example: Naloxone (Narcan) blocks opioid receptors instantly, reversing heroin overdoses — and also blocks endorphins.
points_json.point: Opioid-blocking drugs like naloxone reverse overdoses by knocking drugs off receptors. They also block natural endorphins, briefly removing the body's own pain relief.

summary: The body's own morphine — runner's high, placebo power, and why social laughter eases pain.
title: Endorphins and Pain

points_json.example: Planning your week, making decisions, controlling impulses — all frontal lobe work.
points_json.point: The frontal lobe handles executive functions: planning, decision-making, judgment, and personality. It also contains the motor cortex, which directs voluntary movement.

points_json.example: Broca's area, in the left frontal lobe, produces speech — damage causes halting, effortful talking.
points_json.point: Broca's area manages speech production. People with Broca's aphasia understand language but struggle to speak fluently, producing short, effortful phrases.

points_json.example: Feeling the texture of fabric or knowing where your hands are without looking — that's the parietal lobe.
points_json.point: The parietal lobe processes touch, temperature, pain, and body position. It also handles spatial awareness and math — damage can cause neglect of one side of space.

points_json.example: Recognizing a friend's face in a crowd happens in the temporal lobe's fusiform face area.
points_json.point: The temporal lobe processes hearing and contains the hippocampus (memory) and amygdala (emotion). Wernicke's area here handles language comprehension — damage causes fluent but meaningless speech.

points_json.example: A blow to the back of the head can cause blindness even with perfectly healthy eyes — the occipital lobe processes vision.
points_json.point: The occipital lobe is devoted to vision. Each part maps the visual field precisely. Damage causes visual deficits matching the injured spot.

points_json.example: Your left brain controls your right hand — each hemisphere runs the opposite side of the body.
points_json.point: Motor and sensory pathways cross over: the left hemisphere controls the right body side and vice versa. This contralateral organization is a basic brain rule.

points_json.example: Phineas Gage survived an iron rod through his frontal lobe but his personality changed completely — polite to rude and impulsive.
points_json.point: The famous 1848 case of Phineas Gage proved the frontal lobe's role in personality and impulse control. His intellect survived, but his character transformed.

summary: The four lobes of the cortex — what each does, plus the famous cases that revealed their secrets.
title: Brain Lobes and Functions

points_json.example: Smelling your grandmother's perfume can flood you with childhood memories — the limbic system links smell and emotion directly.
points_json.point: The limbic system is a ring of structures deep in the brain that handles emotion and memory. Unlike other senses, smell connects straight to it, bypassing rational filters.

points_json.example: A sudden rustle in the bushes makes you jump before you even know what it was — your amygdala reacted first.
points_json.point: The amygdala is the brain's threat detector. It triggers fear responses in milliseconds via a 'low road' that bypasses conscious thought — faster than reason, which is why we startle first and think later.

points_json.example: Patient H.M. lost his hippocampus to surgery and could never form new long-term memories again.
points_json.point: The hippocampus forms new explicit memories. H.M.'s 1953 surgery removed it, leaving him unable to remember anything new while old memories stayed — proving memory formation has a specific home.

points_json.example: After eating, when you're cold, or when you're thirsty — the hypothalamus noticed first and drove you to act.
points_json.point: The hypothalamus is the body's control center: hunger, thirst, temperature, sleep, and hormones. It links the nervous system to the endocrine system via the pituitary gland.

points_json.example: Feeling torn between two choices activates the anterior cingulate — it monitors conflict and emotional pain.
points_json.point: The cingulate cortex helps regulate emotions and attention. It activates during social rejection — which is why heartbreak literally registers like physical pain.

points_json.example: Monkeys with amygdala damage (Kluver-Bucy syndrome) lose all fear and try to eat or mate with everything.
points_json.point: Kluver-Bucy syndrome, from amygdala damage, causes fearlessness, hypersexuality, and putting everything in the mouth — showing how much the amygdala normally restrains us.

points_json.example: Meditation practice can shrink amygdala reactivity while strengthening prefrontal control — training emotional balance.
points_json.point: The prefrontal cortex regulates the limbic system top-down. Stronger prefrontal-limbic connections mean better emotion control; weaker ones mean impulsivity and anxiety.

points_json.example: London taxi drivers memorizing 25,000 streets grow larger hippocampi — proof the limbic system physically adapts.
points_json.point: The hippocampus is one of few brain areas that keeps growing new neurons in adulthood, and it physically expands with heavy memory demands like navigating a city.

summary: The emotional brain — amygdala, hippocampus, hypothalamus, and how feelings and memories intertwine.
title: The Limbic System

points_json.example: Epilepsy patients who had their corpus callosum cut found their seizures reduced — and gave science a window into the two hemispheres.
points_json.point: In the 1960s, Sperry and Gazzaniga studied patients whose corpus callosum (the bridge between hemispheres) was cut to treat severe epilepsy. Each hemisphere then worked alone, revealing their specialties.

points_json.example: Show a picture to the right visual field (left brain) and the patient names it easily — language lives mostly on the left.
points_json.point: The left hemisphere usually handles language, logic, and analysis in right-handed people. The right hemisphere excels at spatial skills, faces, music, and emotion.

points_json.example: Flash an image to the left visual field (right brain) and the patient says they saw nothing — but their left hand picks the matching object.
points_json.point: In the classic test, information shown to the right brain couldn't be named (no language there) but could be identified by touch with the left hand — proving knowledge existed without words.

points_json.example: The left brain invents explanations for actions the right brain caused — like a press secretary making up stories.
points_json.point: Gazzaniga called the left hemisphere 'the interpreter' — it constantly creates stories to explain behavior, even when the real cause came from the isolated right brain.

points_json.example: Split-brain patients function surprisingly normally in daily life — the hemispheres find workarounds.
points_json.point: Outside the lab, split-brain patients seem almost normal. Each hemisphere adapts, and everyday tasks rarely require the precise separation that experiments create.

points_json.example: Roger Sperry won the 1981 Nobel Prize for split-brain research, transforming our view of consciousness.
points_json.point: The research earned Sperry a Nobel Prize and showed that consciousness isn't perfectly unified — cutting the connection can create two independent streams of awareness.

points_json.example: The right hemisphere reads facial expressions and tone of voice better — emotional intelligence leans right.
points_json.point: While the left brain handles words, the right brain reads the music of speech — sarcasm, emotion, and facial expressions. Damage to the right hemisphere impairs social understanding.

points_json.example: The 'left-brained logical, right-brained creative' personality myth is oversimplified — both sides collaborate constantly.
points_json.point: Pop culture exaggerates hemispheric differences. In intact brains, the hemispheres work together through 200 million corpus callosum fibers on nearly every task.

summary: What cutting the brain in half revealed — Sperry and Gazzaniga's Nobel-winning split-brain experiments.
title: Split-Brain Research

points_json.example: London cab drivers who memorize 25,000 streets develop measurably larger hippocampi than bus drivers on fixed routes.
points_json.point: Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to rewire itself with experience. Learning a demanding skill physically changes brain structure — the brain is not fixed after childhood.

points_json.example: Neurons that fire together wire together — practicing piano strengthens the exact circuits you use.
points_json.point: Hebb's rule explains the mechanism: when two neurons repeatedly activate together, their connection strengthens. This long-term potentiation (LTP) is the molecular basis of learning.

points_json.example: Blind readers use their visual cortex to read Braille — the brain reassigns unused territory.
points_json.point: When one sense is lost, the brain reallocates. In blind people, the visual cortex processes touch and hearing. The brain hates wasted space.

points_json.example: After a stroke destroyed her language area, a patient slowly regained speech as nearby regions took over the job.
points_json.point: Stroke recovery demonstrates plasticity: surviving neurons sprout new connections and neighboring areas adopt lost functions, especially with intensive rehabilitation.

points_json.example: Rats in toy-filled cages grow thicker cortices with more connections than rats in bare cages.
points_json.point: Enriched environments physically build bigger, better-connected brains in animals. Stimulation, exercise, and social contact all promote neural growth.

points_json.example: Violinists have enlarged brain areas for their left-hand fingers — years of practice reshaped their cortex.
points_json.point: Musicians, jugglers, and meditators all show structural brain changes matching their practice. Even weeks of juggling practice visibly grows relevant brain areas.

points_json.example: Children who miss early language exposure struggle to ever fully catch up — some windows narrow with age.
points_json.point: Plasticity has limits. Critical periods exist for vision and language — missed early input causes lasting deficits. But adult plasticity, though slower, never fully disappears.

points_json.example: Phantom limb pain happens because the brain remaps — the face area invades the missing hand's territory.
points_json.point: After amputation, the cortex reorganizes and the missing limb's area gets taken over — sometimes causing the eerie feeling (and pain) of a phantom limb.

summary: The brain rewires itself — how experience, practice, and injury physically reshape neural circuits.
title: Neuroplasticity

points_json.example: At peak, the fetal brain produces about 250,000 new neurons per minute.
points_json.point: Brain development starts with the neural tube, then explodes: neurons are born, migrate to their positions, and connect. This construction is mostly complete before birth.

points_json.example: Nearly half of all neurons produced before birth die off — the brain overbuilds, then keeps only the useful ones.
points_json.point: Programmed cell death (apoptosis) eliminates up to 50% of neurons. This pruning isn't damage — it's sculpting, removing weak connections to strengthen important ones.

points_json.example: Teenagers lose gray matter as unused childhood synapses are pruned — their brains are streamlining, not shrinking.
points_json.point: Synaptic pruning peaks in adolescence: rarely used connections are cut while frequently used ones strengthen. 'Use it or lose it' is literal neuroscience.

points_json.example: The frontal lobe myelinates last, finishing in the mid-20s — which is why teens are impulsive and adults are steadier.
points_json.point: Myelination continues into the mid-20s, with the prefrontal cortex (judgment, planning) finished last. This developmental lag explains adolescent risk-taking.

points_json.example: Children born with cataracts must have them removed within months, or the visual cortex never learns to see properly.
points_json.point: Sensitive periods are windows when the brain must receive input. Miss the window for vision or language, and full development becomes impossible.

points_json.example: Alcohol during pregnancy can cause fetal alcohol syndrome — lifelong brain damage from a preventable cause.
points_json.point: The developing brain is vulnerable: alcohol, drugs, malnutrition, and severe stress during pregnancy or early childhood can cause lasting damage.

points_json.example: Neglected Romanian orphans showed smaller brains and cognitive delays — but early adoption reversed much of the harm.
points_json.point: Early experience sculpts the brain. Severe neglect shrinks cortical areas, yet the young brain's plasticity means timely rescue can recover remarkable ground.

points_json.example: The hippocampus keeps making new neurons throughout life — learning and exercise boost this neurogenesis.
points_json.point: Development never fully stops. Adult neurogenesis continues in the hippocampus, and learning reshapes connections lifelong — the brain remains a work in progress.

summary: How the brain builds itself — neuron birth, pruning, myelination, and why timing matters so much.
title: Brain Development

points_json.example: Your eye color, height, and much of your temperament trace back to DNA instructions in your chromosomes.
points_json.point: Genes are DNA segments that code for proteins. Humans have 23 chromosome pairs carrying about 20,000 genes — the instruction set for building and running the body and brain.

points_json.example: All humans share 99.9% of their DNA — the tiny 0.1% difference creates all human variety.
points_json.point: Genetic differences between people are small in absolute terms but powerful. Small variations (SNPs) influence traits from disease risk to personality tendencies.

points_json.example: Having a gene doesn't guarantee its effect — stress can switch genes on, while calm environments leave them silent.
points_json.point: Gene expression matters more than gene possession. Environmental factors turn genes on or off, which is why identical genes can produce different outcomes in different lives.

points_json.example: Childhood trauma can add chemical marks to DNA that change stress responses — marks sometimes passed to children.
points_json.point: Epigenetics studies how experience changes gene expression without altering DNA itself. Trauma, diet, and stress can methylate genes, dialing their activity up or down.

points_json.example: Intelligence involves hundreds of genes, each adding a tiny effect — there is no single 'smart gene.'
points_json.point: Most psychological traits are polygenic — influenced by many genes. Height, intelligence, and personality each involve hundreds or thousands of genetic variants.

points_json.example: Huntington's disease comes from one faulty gene and always develops — but such single-gene traits are rare in psychology.
points_json.point: Single-gene disorders like Huntington's or PKU are exceptions. PKU shows environment matters too: a special diet in childhood prevents the brain damage the gene would cause.

points_json.example: Heritability of 60% for a trait means genes explain 60% of differences between people — not that you are 60% genetic.
points_json.point: Heritability is a population statistic about variation, not an individual recipe. It also changes with environment — heritability of IQ is higher in wealthy families with equal opportunities.

summary: DNA to behavior — genes, gene expression, epigenetics, and what heritability really means.
title: Genetics and Behavior Basics

points_json.example: Identical twins share 100% of genes; fraternal twins share about 50% — like regular siblings.
points_json.point: Twin studies compare monozygotic (identical, MZ) twins with dizygotic (fraternal, DZ) twins. Greater similarity in MZ twins points to genetic influence on a trait.

points_json.example: The Minnesota study of twins raised apart found separated identical twins with eerily similar habits, tastes, and even names for their dogs.
points_json.point: The famous Minnesota twin study followed identical twins raised in different families. They showed striking similarities in personality, interests, and quirks — suggesting strong genetic influence.

points_json.example: IQ heritability is roughly 50-80% in adults — genes matter a lot, but so does environment.
points_json.point: Twin research estimates heritability: intelligence around 50-80%, personality traits around 40-50%, and schizophrenia risk strongly genetic. These are population averages, not personal destinies.

points_json.example: Adopted children's IQs resemble their biological parents more than their adoptive parents as they grow older.
points_json.point: Adoption studies separate nature from nurture: children raised by non-relatives. As adoptees age, their traits increasingly match biological relatives — genetic influence grows with age.

points_json.example: Surprisingly, growing up in the same home makes siblings' personalities only slightly more similar.
points_json.point: Shared family environment has modest effects on personality. Non-shared environment — different friends, experiences, even birth order effects — matters more for making siblings different.

points_json.example: A musically gifted child seeks out instruments and lessons — genes steering their own environment.
points_json.point: Gene-environment correlation: our genes influence the environments we choose. An active child joins sports; a shy child avoids parties — genes shape nurture itself.

points_json.example: A child with a 'risk' gene in a loving home may thrive, while the same gene in a harsh home predicts trouble.
points_json.point: Gene-environment interaction: genes and environment multiply each other. The same genetic variant can lead to different outcomes depending on life experience.

points_json.example: Twin studies assume identical and fraternal twins share environments equally — critics say identical twins are treated more alike.
points_json.point: The equal environments assumption is debated: identical twins may share more similar treatment, which could inflate heritability estimates. Researchers test this with twins raised apart.

summary: Nature vs nurture, tested — how twin and adoption studies reveal the genetics of mind and behavior.
title: Twin and Adoption Studies

points_json.example: Giraffes with longer necks reached more food, survived, and passed long-neck genes on — nature's filtering process.
points_json.point: Natural selection: organisms with helpful traits survive and reproduce more, spreading those traits. Over generations, populations adapt to their environments.

points_json.example: Humans everywhere fear snakes and spiders more readily than cars, though cars kill far more people today.
points_json.point: Evolutionary psychology argues the mind has built-in adaptations like the body does. Prepared learning makes us acquire ancient fears (snakes, heights) faster than modern dangers.

points_json.example: Across cultures, men tend to value youth and health cues in mates, women tend to value resources and status — patterns predicted by parental investment theory.
points_json.point: David Buss's cross-cultural research found consistent mate preference patterns. Parental investment theory explains them: the sex investing more in offspring (usually females) is choosier.

points_json.example: Ground squirrels risk their lives giving alarm calls — mostly when relatives are nearby to benefit.
points_json.point: Kin selection (Hamilton's rule): helping relatives spreads your shared genes. Altruism toward kin is genetically 'selfish' — it protects copies of your own genes.

points_json.example: Vampire bats share blood with hungry non-relatives who later return the favor — cooperation among non-kin.
points_json.point: Reciprocal altruism (Trivers): help non-relatives who may repay you. Cheater-detection is key — evolutionary psychologists argue we have mental modules for spotting freeloaders.

points_json.example: Newborns prefer face-like patterns within hours of birth — social interest seems pre-wired.
points_json.point: Some abilities appear too early for learning: face preference, language readiness, and stranger anxiety all emerge on maturational schedules suggesting evolved design.

points_json.example: Critics call evolutionary explanations 'just-so stories' — clever tales that can't be proven wrong.
points_json.point: Evolutionary psychology faces criticism: hypotheses about the ancient past are hard to test, it may underestimate culture, and it risks justifying current inequalities as 'natural.'

points_json.example: People everywhere recognize happy, sad, angry, and fearful faces — Ekman's research found emotional expressions are universal.
points_json.point: Paul Ekman's cross-cultural studies showed basic facial expressions are recognized worldwide, even in isolated tribes — strong evidence for evolved emotional hardware.

summary: The evolved mind — natural selection, mate preferences, altruism, and the debates around evolutionary psychology.
title: Evolution and Behavior

points_json.example: Hormones are the body's slow mail — traveling by blood, taking minutes to act but lasting for hours.
points_json.point: The endocrine system is glands releasing hormones into the bloodstream. Unlike fast neural signals, hormonal messages are slower but longer-lasting and body-wide.

points_json.example: The pituitary is called the master gland because it controls the thyroid, adrenals, and gonads — but the hypothalamus controls the pituitary.
points_json.point: The hypothalamus-pituitary axis is command central. The hypothalamus tells the pituitary what to release, and the pituitary directs other glands — a chain of command.

points_json.example: An underactive thyroid makes people sluggish, cold, and depressed — often mistaken for mental illness.
points_json.point: The thyroid gland sets metabolic speed. Too little thyroid hormone causes fatigue, weight gain, and depression-like symptoms; too much causes anxiety, tremors, and weight loss.

points_json.example: The adrenal glands sit atop the kidneys and release adrenaline for emergencies and cortisol for prolonged stress.
points_json.point: The adrenals have two parts: the medulla releases adrenaline (fast fight-or-flight), the cortex releases cortisol (sustained stress response). Both prepare the body for challenge.

points_json.example: After eating, the pancreas releases insulin to move sugar into cells — diabetics lack this control.
points_json.point: The pancreas regulates blood sugar with insulin (lowers it) and glucagon (raises it). Blood sugar swings affect the brain directly — low sugar causes irritability and confusion.

points_json.example: Testosterone and estrogen from the gonads drive puberty, sexual development, and influence mood and aggression.
points_json.point: The gonads (testes, ovaries) produce sex hormones that organize the body at puberty and continue affecting behavior, energy, and emotion throughout life.

points_json.example: As daylight fades, the pineal gland releases melatonin, telling your body night is coming.
points_json.point: The tiny pineal gland secretes melatonin in darkness, timing sleep. Light suppresses it — which is why screens before bed disrupt sleep.

summary: The body's chemical messengers — glands, hormones, and the master control axis explained simply.
title: The Endocrine System

points_json.example: Exam stress floods your body with cortisol — helpful for a week, harmful for a year.
points_json.point: Cortisol is the main stress hormone from the adrenal cortex. Short bursts mobilize energy; chronically high cortisol damages the hippocampus, weakens immunity, and impairs memory.

points_json.example: Winning a competition raises testosterone — and higher testosterone makes the next challenge feel more winnable.
points_json.point: Testosterone is linked to competitiveness and aggression, but effects are modest and bidirectional: behavior changes hormones as much as hormones change behavior.

points_json.example: A mother's oxytocin surges during childbirth and breastfeeding, promoting bonding with her baby.
points_json.point: Oxytocin promotes trust, bonding, and social connection. It's released during childbirth, nursing, hugging, and warm social contact — though its effects depend heavily on context.

points_json.example: Many women notice mood shifts with their menstrual cycle as estrogen and progesterone rise and fall.
points_json.point: Estrogen and progesterone fluctuate across the menstrual cycle, affecting mood, energy, and cognition. Severe premenstrual mood symptoms (PMDD) are a recognized disorder.

points_json.example: An adrenaline surge lets a mother lift a car to save her child — the legendary 'hysterical strength.'
points_json.point: Adrenaline (epinephrine) from the adrenal medulla drives instant fight-or-flight: heart pounds, airways open, blood rushes to muscles — maximum power in seconds.

points_json.example: Hypothyroidism is routinely misdiagnosed as depression — fixing the thyroid lifts the mood.
points_json.point: Thyroid hormones regulate energy and mood. Low thyroid mimics depression (fatigue, low mood); high thyroid mimics anxiety (jitteriness, racing heart). Always check the thyroid first.

points_json.example: Skipping meals makes many people irritable and foggy — the brain runs almost entirely on glucose.
points_json.point: Insulin and glucagon keep blood sugar steady for the glucose-hungry brain. Drops in blood sugar cause shakiness, irritability, and poor concentration — 'hanger' is biochemistry.

points_json.example: Prenatal testosterone exposure shapes brain development, while adult hormone levels activate current behavior.
points_json.point: Hormones work two ways: organizational effects (permanent, during development) and activational effects (temporary, in the moment). Both shape who we are.

summary: Chemical messengers that shape mood and action — cortisol, testosterone, oxytocin, thyroid, and more.
title: Hormones and Behavior

points_json.example: Rats with lateral hypothalamus damage stop eating entirely; rats with ventromedial damage eat until obese.
points_json.point: Classic lesion studies found the lateral hypothalamus acts as a hunger 'on' switch and the ventromedial hypothalamus as the 'off' switch. Modern research shows the system is far more complex, but the hypothalamus remains central.

points_json.example: Your stomach growls and releases ghrelin before lunch — the hunger hormone announcing mealtime.
points_json.point: Ghrelin, released by an empty stomach, signals hunger to the brain. After eating, fat cells release leptin, signaling fullness. These opposing hormones rhythmically drive appetite.

points_json.example: Many obese people have high leptin but their brains ignore it — leptin resistance, like insulin resistance in diabetes.
points_json.point: In obesity, leptin resistance often develops: plenty of leptin circulates, but the brain stops responding. The result is persistent hunger despite ample fat stores.

points_json.example: Dieters often regain weight because their metabolism slows and hunger hormones surge — the body defends its set point.
points_json.point: Set-point theory: the body defends a weight range. Dieting triggers metabolic slowdown and increased ghrelin — biology fights weight loss, which is why keeping it off is so hard.

points_json.example: Just smelling fresh bread can make you hungry even after a meal — external cues trigger appetite.
points_json.point: Hunger isn't only internal. Sights, smells, and food advertising trigger the cephalic phase — the brain preparing for food before a bite is taken.

points_json.example: Cannon showed that stomach contractions happen with hunger but removing them doesn't eliminate it — hunger lives in the brain.
points_json.point: Early research proved hunger isn't just an empty stomach. Brain signals, blood chemistry, and hormones together create the experience of hunger.

points_json.example: Blood sugar drops are detected by the brain and liver, triggering hunger before energy truly runs out.
points_json.point: Glucostatic theory: falling blood glucose triggers hunger. The liver and brain monitor fuel levels constantly, launching appetite well before crisis.

points_json.example: Anorexia and binge eating involve disrupted hypothalamic signals plus reward circuits and cultural pressures — biology and environment together.
points_json.point: Eating disorders blend biology and psychology: hypothalamic dysregulation, dopamine reward abnormalities, genetics, and cultural thin-ideals all contribute.

summary: How the brain controls appetite — hypothalamus, ghrelin, leptin, set points, and why diets fight biology.
title: Hunger and Eating Regulation

points_json.example: After salty chips, your blood gets saltier and osmoreceptors trigger thirst — your body demanding water to dilute it.
points_json.point: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect concentrated (salty) blood and trigger osmotic thirst. This is why salty food makes you thirsty.

points_json.example: Losing blood triggers a different thirst — the kidneys release renin, starting a hormonal cascade demanding fluids.
points_json.point: Low blood volume triggers hypovolemic thirst: kidneys release renin, producing angiotensin, which signals the brain to drink and conserve water.

points_json.example: ADH tells the kidneys to save water, making urine concentrated — dehydration's dark-yellow signal.
points_json.point: Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) from the pituitary tells kidneys to reabsorb water. More ADH means less water lost — a key defense against dehydration.

points_json.example: You stop feeling thirsty after a few gulps, long before the water reaches your blood — the mouth meters intake in advance.
points_json.point: Oropharyngeal metering: nerves in the mouth and throat signal the brain during drinking, quenching thirst before absorption. The brain predicts hydration needs.

points_json.example: Even mild dehydration — 1-2% water loss — measurably worsens concentration, mood, and reaction time.
points_json.point: The brain is 75% water and exquisitely sensitive to fluid loss. Dehydration impairs cognition, increases headaches, and darkens mood before you feel truly thirsty.

points_json.example: Elderly people feel less thirsty even when dehydrated, raising their risk dangerously in heat waves.
points_json.point: Aging blunts osmoreceptor sensitivity, so older adults under-drink. Caregivers must offer fluids proactively, especially in hot weather.

points_json.example: Alcohol suppresses ADH, so kidneys dump water — the frequent bathroom trips and next-day dehydration of hangovers.
points_json.point: Alcohol inhibits vasopressin release, causing excessive urination. The resulting dehydration drives headaches, fatigue, and thirst — the classic hangover.

summary: The biology of thirst — osmoreceptors, ADH, blood volume signals, and why dehydration clouds thinking.
title: Thirst and Body Fluids

points_json.example: Rats with damage to the medial preoptic area of the hypothalamus lose interest in mating entirely.
points_json.point: The hypothalamus, especially the medial preoptic area, is the command center for sexual behavior. Damage here reduces sexual motivation dramatically in animals.

points_json.example: Testosterone drives sexual desire in both men and women — women's ovaries and adrenal glands produce it too.
points_json.point: Testosterone is the main desire hormone for both sexes. Estrogen and progesterone modulate receptivity, especially across the menstrual cycle.

points_json.example: Prenatal hormone exposure shapes the developing brain — more androgen exposure tends to masculinize later behavior patterns.
points_json.point: Hormones organize the brain before birth. The amount of testosterone a fetus is exposed to influences later gender-typical play, interests, and orientation tendencies.

points_json.example: Masters and Johnson mapped the human sexual response: excitement, plateau, orgasm, resolution — a cycle both sexes share.
points_json.point: The classic four-phase model describes arousal building (excitement), sustained high arousal (plateau), climax (orgasm), and recovery (resolution). Men have a refractory period; many women can have multiple orgasms.

points_json.example: Prairie voles, famously monogamous, have dense vasopressin and oxytocin receptors — their promiscuous cousins don't.
points_json.point: Oxytocin and vasopressin drive pair bonding. Vole studies show receptor density determines monogamy — a beautiful demonstration of neurochemistry shaping love.

points_json.example: Identical twins are more likely to share sexual orientation than fraternal twins, pointing to biological influence.
points_json.point: Twin and family studies show moderate heritability for sexual orientation. Prenatal factors (like the fraternal birth order effect) also play roles. There is no single 'gay gene.'

points_json.example: The claim that humans detect pheromones like animals remains unproven — the vomeronasal organ appears nonfunctional in adults.
points_json.point: Pheromone effects are well-established in animals but debated in humans. Some studies find menstrual synchrony or MHC-related odor preferences, but evidence is weak.

points_json.example: Stress, fatigue, and depression suppress sexual desire through hormonal and neural pathways — the mind and body act as one.
points_json.point: Sexual function reflects whole-body health: cardiovascular fitness, hormones, mood, and relationship quality all interact. Problems often have mixed biological and psychological causes.

summary: The biology of desire — hypothalamus, hormones, prenatal organization, and the science of bonding.
title: Sexual Behavior Biology

points_json.example: Jet lag happens because your suprachiasmatic nucleus is still on home time — light slowly resets it.
points_json.point: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the hypothalamus is the master clock, running a roughly 24-hour circadian rhythm. Light hitting the retina resets it daily.

points_json.example: As evening falls, the pineal gland releases melatonin — but scrolling your phone suppresses it and delays sleep.
points_json.point: Melatonin signals darkness to the body. Blue light from screens suppresses melatonin release, which is why late-night scrolling pushes sleep later.

points_json.example: A full sleep cycle runs about 90 minutes: light sleep, deeper sleep, deepest slow-wave sleep, then REM dreaming.
points_json.point: Sleep stages cycle through N1 (drifting off), N2 (light sleep), N3 (deep slow-wave sleep), and REM (rapid eye movement). We cycle through these 4-6 times per night.

points_json.example: During REM sleep your brain is wildly active while your body is paralyzed — preventing you from acting out dreams.
points_json.point: In REM sleep, the brainstem paralyzes muscles (atonia) while the cortex fires intensely. This is when vivid dreaming occurs.

points_json.example: Deep slow-wave sleep releases growth hormone and consolidates memories — students who sleep after studying remember more.
points_json.point: N3 deep sleep is physically restorative: tissues repair, growth hormone releases, and the immune system strengthens. Memory consolidation also depends on it.

points_json.example: Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors — adenosine is the 'sleep pressure' chemical that builds all day.
points_json.point: The longer you're awake, the more adenosine accumulates, increasing sleepiness. Caffeine masks this signal without removing the underlying tiredness.

points_json.example: After 24 hours awake, judgment and reaction time resemble legal drunkenness — the prefrontal cortex fails first.
points_json.point: Sleep deprivation hits the prefrontal cortex hardest: attention, planning, and impulse control collapse. Microsleeps intrude dangerously, especially while driving.

points_json.example: Night-shift workers face higher rates of obesity, diabetes, and heart disease — chronic circadian disruption harms health.
points_json.point: Shift work desynchronizes the body's clocks, raising risks for metabolic and cardiovascular disease. Timed light exposure and consistent schedules help.

summary: The sleeping brain — circadian clocks, melatonin, sleep stages, and what deprivation does to the mind.
title: Sleep Neuroscience

points_json.example: Hobson argued dreams are the cortex's best effort to make sense of random brainstem signals during REM.
points_json.point: The activation-synthesis hypothesis (Hobson & McCarley) says dreams begin with random neural firing from the pons during REM sleep. The forebrain then weaves these signals into stories.

points_json.example: During REM, the pons fires bursts of signals (PGO waves) that the visual and emotional cortex interprets as dream imagery.
points_json.point: Ponto-geniculo-occipital waves bombard the cortex during REM. The brain's storytelling machinery converts this noise into narrative dreams.

points_json.example: People mostly dream about familiar concerns — exams, relationships, work — not random nonsense.
points_json.point: The continuity hypothesis notes dreams reflect waking life concerns. While activation is random, the content draws on our memories, worries, and desires.

points_json.example: Some dreamers realize they're dreaming and take control — lucid dreaming involves reactivated prefrontal areas.
points_json.point: In lucid dreams, parts of the prefrontal cortex 'wake up' inside the dream, giving self-awareness. Training techniques can increase lucid dreaming frequency.

points_json.example: PTSD nightmares replay trauma with amygdala hyperactivity — the fear system intruding into sleep.
points_json.point: Trauma nightmares involve an overactive amygdala during REM. Prazosin, which dampens noradrenergic activity, can reduce these nightmares.

points_json.example: Freud claimed dreams disguise forbidden wishes (latent content) in symbols (manifest content) — but this lacks biological evidence.
points_json.point: Freud's wish-fulfillment theory dominated for decades but has little neuroscience support. Modern views see dreams as brain activity plus memory processing, not hidden messages.

points_json.example: Sleeping after learning strengthens memories — dreams may be the conscious echo of consolidation work.
points_json.point: The memory consolidation view: REM sleep replays and integrates daily experiences. Dream content may reflect the brain filing memories.

points_json.example: People blind from birth have rich auditory and tactile dreams but no visual imagery.
points_json.point: Congenitally blind dreamers experience sound, touch, and emotion vividly — but no vision. Dream imagery depends on sensory experience, supporting biological accounts.

summary: Why we dream, biologically — activation-synthesis, REM mechanisms, lucid dreams, and nightmares.
title: Dreams: Biological Views

points_json.example: A car backfiring makes you duck before you realize it's harmless — the amygdala's 'low road' beat your thinking brain.
points_json.point: LeDoux showed threat signals reach the amygdala via a fast subcortical 'low road' before the cortex analyzes them. We feel fear before we know why.

points_json.example: Soldiers trained in mindfulness show stronger prefrontal control over amygdala reactivity under stress.
points_json.point: The prefrontal cortex regulates emotion top-down, inhibiting the amygdala. Stronger prefrontal-amygdala connections predict better emotional control and resilience.

points_json.example: James and Lange argued we feel afraid because we tremble — the body's reaction comes first, the feeling follows.
points_json.point: The James-Lange theory: emotions result from perceiving our bodily changes. We don't cry because we're sad — we're sad because we cry. Facial feedback studies partly support this.

points_json.example: Cannon and Bard countered that body and feeling happen together — thalamic signals split to both simultaneously.
points_json.point: The Cannon-Bard theory says emotional experience and bodily arousal occur at the same time, not in sequence. Cutting the link between body and brain wouldn't eliminate emotion, they argued.

points_json.example: In Schachter and Singer's famous study, aroused participants felt happy or angry depending on the situation they were placed in.
points_json.point: The Schachter-Singer two-factor theory: general arousal plus a cognitive label equals a specific emotion. The same racing heart becomes excitement at a party or fear in a dark alley.

points_json.example: EEG studies show left frontal activation with positive moods, right frontal with negative moods and withdrawal.
points_json.point: Hemispheric asymmetry research finds the left prefrontal cortex associated with approach and positive emotion, the right with withdrawal and negative emotion.

points_json.example: Seeing a disgusting image activates the insula — the same region active when you taste something rotten.
points_json.point: The insula processes disgust and interoception (body awareness). The anterior cingulate activates both for our own pain and witnessing others' pain — an empathy circuit.

points_json.example: Forcing a smile can slightly lift your mood — the facial feedback effect, though smaller than once claimed.
points_json.point: Facial expressions feed back into emotional experience. Botox reducing frown muscles has even been studied for mild antidepressant effects.

summary: Where feelings live in the brain — amygdala pathways, the classic emotion theories, and hemispheric asymmetry.
title: Emotion and the Brain

points_json.example: Patient H.M. could learn new motor skills but never remember practicing — his hippocampus was gone.
points_json.point: The hippocampus is essential for forming new explicit (declarative) memories. H.M.'s surgery proved memory formation and memory storage are separate processes.

points_json.example: Where were you during a major national tragedy? Flashbulb memories feel vivid because the amygdala stamped them with emotion.
points_json.point: The amygdala attaches emotional significance to memories. Highly emotional events trigger stronger consolidation — which is why we remember where we were during shocking news.

points_json.example: You can ride a bike years later without thinking — the cerebellum and basal ganglia store procedural memory.
points_json.point: Skill and habit memory lives in the cerebellum (timing, coordination) and basal ganglia (habits). These implicit memories survive even when explicit memory fails.

points_json.example: Holding a phone number in mind while dialing uses prefrontal working memory — easily disrupted by distraction.
points_json.point: The prefrontal cortex maintains working memory — information held briefly for use. Its limited capacity (about 4 chunks) explains why multitasking fails.

points_json.example: When two neurons fire together repeatedly, their synapse strengthens — Hebb's rule, the basis of long-term potentiation.
points_json.point: LTP in the hippocampus is the leading molecular model of memory: repeated activation strengthens synapses via glutamate receptors, making future firing easier.

points_json.example: Sleep after studying moves memories from hippocampus to cortex — all-nighters sabotage this transfer.
points_json.point: Systems consolidation: new memories depend on the hippocampus, then gradually become cortex-dependent over weeks. Sleep, especially deep sleep, drives this transfer.

points_json.example: Adults can't remember anything before age 3 because the hippocampus and language systems were still immature.
points_json.point: Infantile amnesia reflects an underdeveloped hippocampus and lack of language to encode events. Early memories exist implicitly but not as recallable stories.

points_json.example: In Alzheimer's, the hippocampus shrinks early — which is why recent memory fails before old memories.
points_json.point: Alzheimer's disease attacks the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex first, erasing the ability to form new memories while childhood memories linger longest.

summary: How the brain stores experience — hippocampus, amygdala, cerebellum, LTP, and why sleep matters for memory.
title: Memory and the Brain

points_json.example: A sudden scare triggers CRH, then ACTH, then cortisol — the HPA cascade mobilizing your body in seconds to minutes.
points_json.point: The HPA axis: the hypothalamus releases CRH, the pituitary releases ACTH, and the adrenal cortex releases cortisol. This chain coordinates the sustained stress response.

points_json.example: Selye's rats exposed to prolonged stress went through alarm, then resistance, then collapse — the General Adaptation Syndrome.
points_json.point: Hans Selye described three stages: alarm (fight-or-flight activation), resistance (coping while resources drain), and exhaustion (resources depleted, illness follows).

points_json.example: Cortisol raises blood sugar, sharpens focus briefly, and suppresses non-urgent functions like digestion and immunity.
points_json.point: Acute cortisol is adaptive: it frees energy, heightens alertness, and pauses maintenance. The problems begin when the alarm never switches off.

points_json.example: Chronically stressed rats grow smaller hippocampi — and stressed humans show the same shrinkage on brain scans.
points_json.point: Chronic cortisol damages the hippocampus (memory), enlarges the amygdala (fear), and weakens the prefrontal cortex (judgment) — literally remodeling the brain.

points_json.example: Cannon described fight-or-flight; Taylor added tend-and-befriend — under stress, many (especially women) nurture and affiliate.
points_json.point: Beyond fight-or-flight, Taylor's tend-and-befriend response involves oxytocin driving social bonding under stress. Social support becomes a biological stress buffer.

points_json.example: Allostatic load is the wear and tear of repeated stress cycles — measured in blood pressure, cortisol, and inflammation.
points_json.point: McEwen's allostatic load concept quantifies chronic stress damage across body systems. High load predicts heart disease, depression, and early mortality.

points_json.example: Two people face the same deadline: the one who feels in control shows far smaller cortisol spikes.
points_json.point: Perceived control powerfully moderates stress physiology. Uncontrollable, unpredictable stressors cause the most HPA damage — control is protective.

points_json.example: Cortisol follows a daily rhythm — peaking at waking (the cortisol awakening response) and falling at night.
points_json.point: Healthy HPA function shows a strong morning peak and evening trough. Flattened rhythms — from shift work or burnout — signal dysregulation.

summary: The body's stress command chain — HPA axis, Selye's stages, cortisol's effects, and tend-and-befriend.
title: Stress Physiology (HPA Axis)

points_json.example: Ader paired sweet water with an immunosuppressant in rats — later, sweet water alone suppressed their immune systems.
points_json.point: Psychoneuroimmunology began when Robert Ader showed the immune system could be classically conditioned. The brain and immune system are in constant two-way communication.

points_json.example: Caregivers of Alzheimer's patients heal wounds significantly slower and respond weaker to vaccines than matched controls.
points_json.point: Chronic stress suppresses immune function measurably: stressed caregivers show slower wound healing, weaker vaccine responses, and higher inflammation.

points_json.example: When you're sick you feel tired, withdrawn, and gloomy — cytokines telling the brain to rest and recover.
points_json.point: Immune messengers called cytokines signal the brain, producing 'sickness behavior': fatigue, social withdrawal, low appetite, and depressed mood. It's adaptive energy conservation.

points_json.example: Some depressed patients have elevated inflammatory markers — and anti-inflammatory drugs sometimes lift their mood.
points_json.point: The inflammation-depression link: elevated cytokines (like IL-6) appear in many depressed patients. Inflammation may cause depressive symptoms, not just accompany them.

points_json.example: The vagus nerve carries immune signals from gut to brain — the 'inflammatory reflex' highway.
points_json.point: The vagus nerve is a major immune-brain channel. It senses inflammation in the body and relays it to the brain; stimulating it can reduce inflammation.

points_json.example: Lonely people show weaker immune responses and higher inflammation than socially connected peers.
points_json.point: Social isolation impairs immunity while strong relationships enhance it. Loneliness is as potent an immune suppressor as chronic stress.

points_json.example: Moderate exercise boosts immune surveillance, while extreme overtraining temporarily suppresses it.
points_json.point: Exercise immunology: regular moderate activity strengthens immunity, but marathon-level exertion opens a temporary window of vulnerability to infections.

points_json.example: Good sleepers produce more antibodies after vaccination than poor sleepers — sleep is immune medicine.
points_json.point: Sleep powerfully supports immunity: even one bad night reduces natural killer cell activity. Vaccines work better in well-rested people.

summary: How mind and immunity talk — psychoneuroimmunology, cytokines, stress, and sickness behavior.
title: Immune-Brain Connection

points_json.example: EEG caps record the brain's electrical chatter in milliseconds — perfect for tracking sleep stages or seizures.
points_json.point: EEG measures electrical activity through scalp electrodes. Its timing is superb (milliseconds) but location is blurry. It's the go-to for sleep research and epilepsy.

points_json.example: CT scans use X-rays to image the brain in minutes — ideal for emergency bleeding, but with radiation exposure.
points_json.point: Computed tomography stacks X-ray slices into a 3D image. It's fast and great for trauma and strokes, but involves radiation and shows soft tissue poorly.

points_json.example: MRI's powerful magnets align hydrogen atoms, producing stunningly detailed brain images with no radiation.
points_json.point: Magnetic resonance imaging offers exquisite structural detail — gray vs white matter, tiny lesions. Downsides: loud, slow, expensive, and impossible with metal implants.

points_json.example: fMRI tracks blood oxygen changes (BOLD signal) to show which areas work harder during tasks.
points_json.point: Functional MRI reveals active brain regions by detecting oxygen use. But it's slow (seconds per image), correlational, and the colorful blobs oversimplify complex activity.

points_json.example: PET scans inject radioactive tracers to map metabolism or specific neurotransmitter receptors.
points_json.point: Positron emission tomography shows brain chemistry in action — glucose use, dopamine receptors. It's invasive (radioactivity) and expensive, but uniquely informative.

points_json.example: Phineas Gage's accident was nature's lesion study — the iron rod's path revealed frontal lobe functions.
points_json.point: The lesion method infers function from damage: lose an area, lose its function. Classic cases like Gage and H.M. founded neuropsychology.

points_json.example: TMS uses magnetic pulses to briefly stimulate or disrupt brain areas — testing causality, not just correlation.
points_json.point: Transcranial magnetic stimulation can temporarily activate or inhibit cortex through the skull. It tests whether an area is necessary for a function — and treats depression.

points_json.example: No scan reads minds — every technique trades off timing, location, invasiveness, and cost.
points_json.point: Each method has blind spots: EEG is fast but blurry, fMRI is sharp but slow, PET is chemical but radioactive. Converging evidence across methods is the gold standard.

summary: Seeing the living brain — EEG, CT, MRI, fMRI, PET, and what each can and cannot show.
title: Brain Imaging Techniques

points_json.example: FAST: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency — stroke signs everyone should know.
points_json.point: Stroke cuts blood to brain regions, killing neurons within minutes. FAST recognition and rapid treatment (clot-busters within hours) save brain tissue and lives.

points_json.example: A concussion is the brain sloshing inside the skull — even 'mild' TBIs can have lasting effects.
points_json.point: Traumatic brain injury ranges from concussion to severe damage. The frontal and temporal lobes, near bony ridges, are most vulnerable. Repeated concussions accumulate harm.

points_json.example: After a stroke, undamaged areas temporarily shut down from lost input (diaschisis), then gradually come back online.
points_json.point: Diaschisis explains early recovery: connected regions go quiet when their partners are damaged, then reactivate. This accounts for rapid initial improvement.

points_json.example: Broca's aphasia: halting, effortful speech ('Want... coffee'). Wernicke's: fluent but meaningless ('The shimmer flapped greenly').
points_json.point: Left-hemisphere strokes often cause aphasia. Broca's (frontal) damages production; Wernicke's (temporal) damages comprehension. The contrast reveals language's division of labor.

points_json.example: Right parietal damage can make patients ignore their entire left side — even denying their own left arm.
points_json.point: Hemispatial neglect: patients eat only the right half of plates and shave only half their faces. It shows attention, not just vision, constructs our world.

points_json.example: Constraint-induced therapy forces stroke patients to use the weak arm by restraining the good one — driving rewiring.
points_json.point: Rehabilitation exploits plasticity: intensive, forced use of impaired functions rebuilds circuits. Timing matters — early, intense therapy works best.

points_json.example: Children recover language after left-hemisphere damage far better than adults — young brains reassign functions.
points_json.point: Younger brains show greater plasticity, but adult recovery is real too. Motivation, intensity of therapy, and social support all predict outcomes.

points_json.example: Amputees feel their missing hand when their cheek is touched — the face area invaded the hand's cortical territory.
points_json.point: Ramachandran's phantom limb work showed dramatic cortical remapping after amputation. Mirror therapy, using visual feedback, can even relieve phantom pain.

summary: When the brain is injured — stroke, TBI, aphasia, neglect, and the remarkable science of recovery.
title: Brain Damage and Recovery

points_json.example: Caffeine blocks adenosine (an agonist would mimic it) — understanding agonist vs antagonist unlocks all drug actions.
points_json.point: Agonists enhance neurotransmitter action (mimicking or boosting it); antagonists block it. Nearly every psychoactive drug is one or the other at specific receptors.

points_json.example: SSRIs block serotonin reuptake, but mood lifts only after weeks — the delay reflects slow receptor adaptations.
points_json.point: SSRIs increase synaptic serotonin immediately, yet depression lifts in 2-6 weeks. The therapeutic effect comes from downstream changes: receptor sensitivity shifts and hippocampal neurogenesis.

points_json.example: Antipsychotics block dopamine D2 receptors — hallucinations fade, but stiffness and tremor can appear.
points_json.point: First-generation antipsychotics powerfully block D2, treating psychosis but causing Parkinson-like movement side effects. Newer drugs balance dopamine and serotonin blockade.

points_json.example: Valium enhances GABA's calming effect within minutes — effective for panic, but dependence builds in weeks.
points_json.point: Benzodiazepines amplify GABA, providing rapid anxiety relief and sedation. Tolerance and dependence develop quickly, making them short-term tools, not long-term solutions.

points_json.example: ADHD stimulants raise dopamine and norepinephrine — paradoxically calming hyperactive children by boosting control circuits.
points_json.point: Methylphenidate and amphetamines increase catecholamines, strengthening prefrontal regulation. The 'paradoxical' calming reflects improved executive control, not sedation.

points_json.example: Lithium steadies bipolar mood swings but requires blood monitoring — the dose helping mania is close to the toxic dose.
points_json.point: Lithium remains a gold-standard mood stabilizer with a narrow therapeutic window. Regular blood tests prevent toxicity affecting kidneys and thyroid.

points_json.example: Heavy drinkers need more alcohol for the same buzz (tolerance) and shake without it (withdrawal) — the brain adapted.
points_json.point: Tolerance: the brain counter-adapts to chronic drug presence, needing more for the same effect. Withdrawal: removing the drug unmasks the counter-adaptation — rebound symptoms.

points_json.example: Placebo painkillers trigger real endorphin release — belief itself is neurochemistry.
points_json.point: The placebo effect involves genuine neurochemical changes: endorphins for pain, dopamine for Parkinson's symptoms. Expectation physically reshapes brain activity.

summary: How brain drugs work — agonists, antagonists, antidepressants, antipsychotics, tolerance, and the placebo effect.
title: Psychopharmacology Basics
